presentingComplaint: Three days of mild bifrontal headache and intermittently blurred vision; otherwise feels well and walked into the department unaided.
history: Known hypertension for 6 years, self-discontinued amlodipine and telmisartan ~4 months ago citing cost and feeling well. No prior specialist follow-up. Denies chest pain, breathlessness, orthopnoea, focal weakness, speech disturbance, seizure or vomiting. No recreational stimulant use, no OTC decongestants, no NSAID or licorice ingestion. Non-smoker, occasional alcohol. No prior renal disease known. Because symptoms are so mild he nearly did not attend - the presentation could easily be mistaken for uncomplicated hypertensive urgency, but the combination of grade III/IV retinal changes, new dipstick proteinuria and a rising creatinine confirms acute target-organ damage and therefore a true hypertensive emergency (accelerated/malignant phase) at an early stage.
examination: Alert, fully oriented, GCS 15, comfortable at rest and not distressed. No focal neurological deficit, no neck stiffness. Fundoscopy: bilateral flame-shaped retinal haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and early blurring of the optic disc margins (accelerated/malignant hypertensive retinopathy, Keith-Wagener grade III progressing to IV). Cardiovascular: forceful apex beat, loud A2, no added sounds, no pulmonary crackles, no peripheral oedema. Abdomen soft, no renal bruit appreciated. Peripheral pulses symmetric with no radio-radial or radio-femoral delay.

labs.blood_film: occasional schistocytes, no established microangiopathic haemolysis
labs.urinalysis: protein 2+, no significant haematuria, no casts

imaging: ECG: voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy with lateral strain pattern, no acute ischaemic changes. Chest X-ray: borderline cardiomegaly, clear lung fields, no pulmonary oedema. Non-contrast CT head (to exclude haemorrhage given headache): no intracranial bleed, no established posterior white-matter oedema of PRES.
microbiology: Not applicable (non-infective presentation). No cultures indicated.
differentialDiagnoses: Uncomplicated hypertensive urgency (excluded - acute target-organ damage present)
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (headache + disc changes, but BP and retinal haemorrhages point to malignant hypertension)
finalDiagnosis: Hypertensive emergency - accelerated/malignant hypertension with grade III/IV retinopathy and acute hypertension-mediated renal injury (early/mild symptomatic phase).
citations: ACC/AHA - Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure (Hypertensive Emergencies) - 2017
ESC/ESH - Guidelines for the Management of Arterial Hypertension (Hypertensive Emergencies) - 2023
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Hypertensive Vascular Disease / Hypertensive Emergencies
contraindications: Avoid rapid or excessive BP reduction: lower mean arterial pressure by no more than ~25% in the first hour to prevent watershed cerebral, coronary or renal hypoperfusion.
Avoid immediate-release / sublingual nifedipine (uncontrolled precipitous drop in BP).
Avoid abrupt normalisation of BP in the setting of chronic hypertension with autoregulatory shift.
edgeCases: Mild symptoms can lead to misclassification as hypertensive urgency and inappropriate outpatient discharge - fundoscopy and urinalysis reclassify it as an emergency.
Malignant-phase hypertension can trigger a microangiopathic picture (schistocytes, LDH rise) mimicking a primary thrombotic microangiopathy.
Secondary causes (phaeochromocytoma, renovascular disease) must be screened once BP is controlled, especially in a patient this age with severe hypertension.
expectedMaiK: Severe hypertension with acute hypertension-mediated organ damage (retinal haemorrhages/early papilloedema, new proteinuria, acute creatinine rise) defines a hypertensive emergency requiring controlled IV BP reduction, not oral outpatient management - distinguish from hypertensive urgency by presence of acute target-organ damage.
expectedNextQuestions: Antihypertensive adherence and reason for stopping medication?
Any chest pain, breathlessness, focal neurological or visual symptoms suggesting other organ involvement?
Recreational stimulant, decongestant, NSAID or licorice use?
Symptoms suggesting secondary hypertension (episodic palpitations/sweating/headache, flank bruit)?
expectedInvestigations: Dilated fundoscopy for hypertensive retinopathy grading
12-lead ECG and chest X-ray for cardiac target-organ damage
Serum creatinine/urea/electrolytes and urinalysis with protein quantification
Blood film, LDH, haptoglobin, platelets to assess microangiopathy
Non-contrast CT head to exclude intracranial haemorrhage
Secondary hypertension screen (plasma/urine metanephrines, renal imaging) once stabilised
regressionAssertions: Presence of acute target-organ damage (grade III/IV retinopathy, new proteinuria, acute creatinine rise) reclassifies from hypertensive urgency to hypertensive emergency despite mild symptoms.
Management requires controlled IV BP reduction with MAP lowered by no more than ~25% in the first hour.
Secondary hypertension screen recommended after stabilisation.
